summary: Defines an IPv6 Address Specific BGP Extended Community attribute. RFC 4360 had only an IPv4 version, which is a problem for applications that need to tag routes with an IPv6 address. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds a BGP extended community that can identify an IPv6 address. It lets applications that use address-specific communities work in an IPv6-only environment.

subtitle: Adds an IPv6-addressed BGP extended community for IPv6-only environments.

tldr.problem: BGP extended communities support IPv4 addresses but not IPv6 addresses, which limits applications that need to work in a pure IPv6 environment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new optional, transitive BGP attribute containing 20-octet communities with a 16-octet IPv6 global administrator field and a 2-octet local administrator field.
tldr.outcome: The new attribute allows address-specific extended communities to carry IPv6 addresses. Unit metadata lists later updates by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

today: RFC 5701 is listed as a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Add an IPv6 Community
sections.content:
BGP Extended Communities previously supported an IPv4 Address Specific Extended Community, but not an equivalent for IPv6. An application using the IPv4 form could therefore lack a matching mechanism in a pure IPv6 environment.

The existing extended-community attribute fixes each community at 8 octets, which is not enough for an IPv6 address-specific community. This RFC defines a separate BGP attribute for the IPv6 form.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv4 address-specific community cannot carry an IPv6 address. This RFC adds a separate form for applications that need IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Attribute and Community Fields
sections.content:
The IPv6 Address Specific Extended Community Attribute is optional and transitive. It contains a set of communities, and routes carrying the attribute belong to the communities listed in it.

Each community is 20 octets: a type octet, a subtype octet, a 16-octet global administrator field holding an IPv6 unicast address, and a 2-octet local administrator field. The subtype determines the meaning of the local value.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attribute groups routes with named communities. Each community carries an IPv6 address and a smaller value whose meaning depends on its subtype.

sections.title: Types and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The first octet indicates whether the community subtype is transitive across Autonomous Systems: 0x00 means transitive and 0x40 means non-transitive. The next octet identifies the subtype, using the same subtypes as the IPv4 Address Specific Extended Community.

The RFC assigns BGP attribute value 25 and defines an IANA registry. It assigns type 0x0002 to IPv6 address-specific Route Target and 0x0003 to IPv6 address-specific Route Origin.
sections.plainLanguage: The type says whether the community can cross autonomous-system boundaries, and the subtype says what it represents. IANA maintains the subtype registry and the RFC assigns values for Route Target and Route Origin.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says this attribute adds no new security issues beyond those that apply to BGP Extended Communities. It warns that a malformed optional transitive attribute can raise a serious issue and refers to the handling discussed for that case.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attribute inherits the security considerations of BGP extended communities. The RFC also calls out the need to handle malformed optional transitive attributes.
